issue_context.title: Potential issues in RegexCache
issue_context.body:
I found two potential issues in `RegexCache` through code review:

1. Should `s_maxCacheSize` not be volatile? It is being written concurrently with read usages. I believe, this works in practice the way the code is written but the JIT would be allowed to just cache one value of this field on a certain thread and reuse that indefinitely. For example, a loop `while (s_maxCacheSize == 15) ;` would potentially never be broken by `s_maxCacheSize = 16;`. This code does not exist, but it demonstrates the potential correctness issue.

2. In some cases, a list is sorted by timestamp:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/5877e8b713742b6d80bd1aa9819094be029e3e1f/src/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/src/System/Text/RegularExpressions/Regex.Cache.cs#L89

When timestamps change this can mean that the comparison function no longer fulfills the contract. This can cause the sorting to crash, loop infinitely or corrupt the list.

>  It is being written concurrently with read usages

Which read are you concerned about? With the exception of one fast-path read, all others are inside the same lock that's held while mutating it, and that fast-path read isn't a problem. And if you mean someone setting the public CacheSize on one thread and reading it in a tight loop on another, that's simply not a real scenario to accommodate. But it also wouldn't hurt to make it volatile or take the lock, since practically no one ever reads the property. 

> When timestamps change this can mean that the comparison function no longer fulfills the contract.

Yes, that could in theory be an issue. In practice it would require setting CacheSize to a smaller value than the number of regexes currently cached, doing so while other threads are processing regexes, and doing so in a way that changed the relative ordering of the timestamps. This isn't how CacheSize is invariably used, which is (if it's used at all) setting it at the beginning of the process and never changing it again. And even if it did occur, it is unlikely to actually cause a problem, as the list needn't be perfectly sorted, so the only truly problematic case would be if it reordered things in such a way that the sorting incurred an out of bounds access. Even so, it's reasonable to fix at some point.

> Which read are you concerned about?

I'm unconcerned in a practical sense as well. That said, I believe it is good practice to keep a codebase free from concurrency issues. In my experience, seemingly harmless and exceedingly rare bugs can bite at some point. So I wanted to bring it to the team's attention on general grounds.

The reason I reviewed the code was that a .NET blog post pointed out the locking improvements in the cache. I wanted to see how this was achieved in order to learn.

review_comments: Can you explain why locking a read to an int is necessary?
Oh, I see the issue. Hmm, pretty hard to reason about whether we might overlook this possibility in other contexts.
